questions.stem: Accounting is best described as:
options: keeping a list of the business's customers and the products each one has bought
counting the cash in the till at the end of each trading day before banking it
recording, reporting and analysing financial information so users can make decisions
calculating the income tax that a business owes the Australian Taxation Office each year
questions.explanation: Accounting covers the whole process of collecting, recording, reporting and interpreting financial information for decision making. Tax calculations and cash counts are parts of a business's activities, not the definition of accounting.

questions.stem: Why does accounting information inform the practices of financial management of a business?
options: it is needed only once a year, when the owner lodges a personal tax return
it shows the owner how cash, costs and profit are tracking, so problems can be fixed early
it guarantees that the business will make a profit in every single future reporting period
it removes any need for the owner to make judgements about the business's future
questions.explanation: Regular accounting reports let owners monitor performance and make informed decisions about pricing, spending, borrowing and growth. Information supports judgement but cannot guarantee profit.

questions.stem: A partnership is a business that:
options: is owned by shareholders who each have limited liability
is owned and run by the government for the public
has a single owner who keeps all of its profits
is owned by two or more people who share its profits
questions.explanation: A partnership has two or more owners who agree to share profits and losses. Shareholders with limited liability own a company, and a single owner is a sole trader.

questions.stem: Kai and Ruby run a café as partners. The café cannot pay a $40,000 debt, and Ruby has no personal assets. What is Kai's position?
options: Kai's liability is limited to the capital he contributed to the café
Kai can be required to pay the whole debt from his personal assets
Kai can be required to pay only half the debt, as his share of the business
Kai has no liability, because a partnership is a separate legal entity
questions.explanation: Partners usually have unlimited liability and are jointly and severally liable, so each can be pursued for all of the partnership's debts. A partnership is not a separate legal entity, so the partners' personal assets are at risk.

questions.stem: A shareholder is:
options: a lender who has given the company a long-term loan
an employee who manages the company's daily operations
a customer who buys goods from the company on credit
a part-owner of a company through the shares they hold
questions.explanation: Shareholders own a company in proportion to their shares and may receive dividends. Lenders are creditors, and managers may or may not be shareholders.

questions.stem: What do the endings 'Pty Ltd' and 'Ltd' in a company's name tell you?
options: Pty Ltd is a public company; Ltd is a private (proprietary) company
Pty Ltd is a private (proprietary) company; Ltd is a public company
Pty Ltd is a partnership; Ltd is a sole trader with limited liability
Pty Ltd is a government business; Ltd is a not-for-profit association
questions.explanation: Proprietary (private) companies end in Pty Ltd and cannot offer shares to the general public, while public companies end in Ltd and can. Both have limited liability for their shareholders.

questions.stem: Which statement shows that a company is a separate legal entity?
options: the company can own property and be sued in its own name
the company's owners are personally liable for all its debts
the company ends when any one of its shareholders dies
the company's profit is taxed in each shareholder's personal return
questions.explanation: As a separate legal entity, a company owns assets, enters contracts and can sue or be sued in its own name, and it continues when shareholders change. A sole trader's business has none of these features.

questions.stem: How do the activities of a trading business differ from those of a service business?
options: it buys and resells goods, so it holds inventories and reports Cost of Goods Sold
it provides services for fees, so it holds no assets other than cash at bank
it never sells to customers on credit, so it has no accounts receivable
it pays no GST on its purchases, because inventory is GST-free
questions.explanation: A trading business earns revenue by selling goods it has bought, so inventories and the cost of goods sold are key accounts. Service businesses earn fees and can also sell on credit and own assets.

questions.stem: Accounts payable are:
options: goods the business holds for resale to its customers
amounts the business owes to its suppliers for credit purchases
amounts owed to the business by its credit customers
cash payments the business has already made to suppliers
questions.explanation: Accounts payable are current liabilities to suppliers. Amounts owed by customers are accounts receivable, and goods held for resale are inventories.

questions.stem: In a trading business, Cost of Goods Sold represents:
options: the cost price of the inventory sold during the period
the selling price of all the inventory on hand at year end
the cash paid to suppliers for inventory during the period
the total of all expenses, including wages and rent
questions.explanation: Cost of Goods Sold is the cost of inventory that has been sold, matched against sales revenue. Cash paid to suppliers can differ because of credit purchases and changes in inventory levels.

questions.stem: Buying shares in a listed company gives an investor a possible return through:
options: fixed interest set by the investor's bank
wages earned by working in the company
dividends and growth in the share price
rent and growth in the value of land
questions.explanation: Shareholders may receive dividends from profits and benefit if the share price rises, though neither is guaranteed. Rent is the return on property, and fixed interest is the return on a term deposit.

questions.stem: Which is a main reason people invest their money in their own business rather than in a term deposit?
options: no need to keep any accounting records or lodge any tax returns
the chance of a higher return, plus independence and income from their own work
a guaranteed return that is always higher than any bank deposit or share investment available
less risk, because a small business cannot make a loss in its first few years
questions.explanation: Owning a business offers potential for higher returns and personal control, but with greater risk than a term deposit. Losses are possible, and records must still be kept.

questions.stem: An investor may need her money back at short notice. Compared with owning a small business or a rental property, why might shares in a listed company suit her better?
options: listed shares are guaranteed by the government against any loss
listed shares can usually be sold quickly on the stock exchange
listed shares always rise in value faster than businesses or property
listed shares pay a fixed amount of interest every month
questions.explanation: Listed shares are liquid because they can normally be sold within days, whereas selling a business or property takes time. Share prices can fall, so shares are not guaranteed.

questions.stem: How would a bank typically use a business's financial statements?
options: to decide how much the owner should take as drawings
to calculate the wages of the business's employees
to judge whether the business can make interest and loan repayments
to set the prices the business charges its customers
questions.explanation: Lenders assess profit, cash flow and existing debts to decide whether a loan can be repaid. Pricing, drawings and wages are decisions for the owner.

questions.stem: The Statement of Profit or Loss reports:
options: assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a particular date
the cash inflows and outflows for a period by activity
a list of all ledger account balances to check double entry
revenue, expenses and the net profit or net loss for a period
questions.explanation: The Statement of Profit or Loss measures performance over a period. Assets, liabilities and equity at a date are in the Statement of Financial Position, and cash flows are in the Statement of Cash Flows.

questions.stem: The Statement of Financial Position reports:
options: the amount of GST owed for the most recent quarter
assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a particular date
revenue earned and expenses incurred over the whole period
cash received and paid over the period by activity
questions.explanation: The Statement of Financial Position shows what the business owns, owes and the owner's claim at one point in time, following the accounting equation.

questions.stem: A business made a net loss for the year. This means that:
options: its cash payments for the period were greater than its cash receipts
its liabilities at year end were greater than its assets
its owner took more drawings than the business earned
its expenses for the period were greater than its revenue
questions.explanation: A net loss occurs when expenses exceed revenue. Cash payments exceeding receipts is a fall in cash, which is a different measure, and liabilities exceeding assets means negative equity.

questions.stem: Which best describes the relationship between income and revenue?
options: revenue is income from ordinary activities; income also includes gains such as on selling an asset
income and revenue mean exactly the same thing and can always be used in place of each other
income is cash received from any source, while revenue includes only the owner's capital contributions
revenue includes loans received, while income includes only sales made on credit to customers
questions.explanation: Income is the broad term for increases in equity other than owner contributions. Revenue is the part arising from ordinary activities such as sales or fees, while gains like a profit on sale of an asset are other income. Loans and contributions are not income.

questions.stem: How does earning a net profit affect the accounting equation?
options: only cash at bank changes, so the equation is unaffected
owner's equity increases, so assets less liabilities increases
liabilities increase by the same amount as the profit earned
assets and liabilities increase, with no change in equity
questions.explanation: Profit belongs to the owner, so it increases owner's equity, and assets less liabilities rises by the same amount. Profit may be held in assets other than cash, such as accounts receivable.

questions.stem: At the start of the year a business had assets of $80,000 and liabilities of $30,000. At the end it had assets of $95,000 and liabilities of $32,000. The owner made no contributions or drawings. What was the net profit?
questions.explanation: Opening equity = 80,000 − 30,000 = $50,000; closing equity = 95,000 − 32,000 = $63,000. With no contributions or drawings, profit = 63,000 − 50,000 = $13,000. Looking only at the rise in assets gives $15,000.

questions.stem: For the same business, suppose the owner had also contributed $5,000 of capital and taken drawings of $10,000 during the year. What would the net profit have been?
questions.explanation: Profit = change in equity + drawings − contributions = 13,000 + 10,000 − 5,000 = $18,000. Drawings reduced equity, so they are added back, and the contribution increased equity without being profit, so it is deducted.

questions.stem: A new business earned fees of $60,000 for the year, of which $8,000 was still owed by customers at year end. Its expenses of $41,000 were all paid in cash. What were its net profit and net cash from operations?
options: net profit $27,000; net cash from operations $11,000
net profit $19,000; net cash from operations $11,000
net profit $11,000; net cash from operations $19,000
net profit $19,000; net cash from operations $19,000
questions.explanation: Profit = 60,000 − 41,000 = $19,000, because fees are revenue when earned. Cash received = 60,000 − 8,000 = $52,000, so net cash from operations = 52,000 − 41,000 = $11,000.

questions.stem: Why can a business report a net profit but have less cash at the end of the year?
options: cash at bank is reported in the Statement of Profit or Loss as an expense
depreciation reduces cash at bank every time it is recorded
it may have sold on credit, bought assets or repaid loans, none of which are expenses
net profit is calculated only from cash received and paid, so the two figures must always agree
questions.explanation: Profit is measured on an accrual basis, so credit sales count before cash arrives, while asset purchases, loan repayments and drawings use cash without being expenses. Depreciation reduces profit but not cash.

questions.stem: The role of an auditor is to:
options: prepare the business's journal entries and post its ledger accounts at the end of each day
decide which products the business should sell and at what prices
lend money to the business when its cash balance falls too low
independently examine financial statements and report whether they present a true and fair view
questions.explanation: An auditor is independent of the business and gives an opinion on whether the statements fairly present its financial performance and position. Recording transactions is the work of bookkeepers and accountants.

questions.stem: Why do shareholders in a public company rely on an independent audit of its financial statements?
options: the audit means the company does not need to keep source documents
the statements are prepared by managers, while most shareholders are not involved in running the company
the audit guarantees that the company's share price will rise in the coming year
the auditor chooses the dividend that every shareholder will receive
questions.explanation: Because managers prepare the reports and shareholders are outsiders, an independent opinion increases confidence that the figures are reliable. An audit gives no guarantee of future share prices.

questions.stem: In a public company's Statement of Financial Position, retained earnings are:
options: loans received from shareholders that must be repaid
profits kept in the company rather than paid out as dividends
cash held at the bank to pay next year's income tax
amounts owed to the company by its credit customers
questions.explanation: Retained earnings are accumulated profits not distributed to shareholders, and they form part of shareholders' equity. They are not a cash balance or a liability.

questions.stem: Which account would appear in a public company's records but never in a sole trader's?
options: Share Capital
Accounts Receivable
Inventories
Depreciation Expense
questions.explanation: Share Capital records the amount shareholders have paid for their shares. A sole trader records the owner's investment in a Capital account instead, while receivables, inventories and depreciation can appear in both.

questions.stem: Which statement about the assets and liabilities of a sole trader and a public company is correct?
options: both can have the same types of assets and liabilities; their equity sections differ
a sole trader can have no non-current assets, while a public company must have them
a public company has no liabilities, because shareholders have limited liability
a sole trader reports the owner's private house as a business asset
questions.explanation: Both kinds of entity can own equipment, hold inventories and borrow; the difference is in equity, where a sole trader shows capital and drawings and a company shows share capital and retained earnings. Limited liability does not mean a company has no debts.
